\chapter{From When, For How Long, And All At Once}
\label{ch:desde-y-de-repente}
\hlchaptermodality{356}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say desde, la cita, la etapa, la ocasion and de repente, and mark when something starts, how long it runs and how fast it arrives.}

Complete ES-C356-repente: say when a thing starts, name the time you agreed on, and say that something arrived without warning.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[desde]{desde — three prepositions stacked into one}

\label{lesson:ES-C356-desde}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the corner}, then \emph{the back}. (\emph{El rincón}; \emph{el fondo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hasta — the word it pairs with.
  \item después — built out of the same parts.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DES-de}, two beats with the weight on the first. The final \emph{d} is soft, nearly a breath. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{desde} — \textquotedblleft{}from,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}since.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's small words wore out. \textbf{Dē} on its own had been carrying too much for too long, and by the time Spanish was forming it could no longer be heard to mean any one thing. So speakers propped it up with another, and then with a third.

\textbf{Desde} is \emph{dē} + \emph{ex} + \emph{dē}. Three prepositions, all doing the same job, fused into one word of two beats.

You have already met the trick without being told: \textbf{después} is \emph{dē} + \emph{ex} + \emph{post}. Same first two pieces, different third.

English does exactly this and nobody blinks: \emph{from out of the house}, \emph{out from behind the door}. Three little words where one used to do.

\textbf{Desde} marks the point a thing starts from, in time or in space, and it wants \textbf{hasta} on the other end. \emph{Desde} the beginning \emph{hasta} the end.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The word that opens a stretch of time, and the pair that closes it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{desde}
  \item \emph{desde hoy}
  \item \emph{desde las tres hasta las cinco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many Latin prepositions are inside \emph{desde}? (Three.) And which word does it want at the other end of a stretch? (\emph{Hasta}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cita]{la cita — the hour you were summoned to}

\label{lesson:ES-C356-cita}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the back of the room}, then \emph{from}. (\emph{El fondo}; \emph{desde}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la agenda — where you write it down.
  \item la hora — what it needs to exist.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SI-ta}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cita} — \textquotedblleft{}the appointment,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the quotation.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ciēre} is to set in motion. Its frequentative, \textbf{citāre}, is to keep setting in motion — which in practice meant to summon: to call a person and require them to appear.

English took the calling and kept four shades of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to \textbf{cite} a source is to summon it to appear in your argument;
  \item to \textbf{recite} is to summon it again, out loud;
  \item to \textbf{incite} a crowd is to set it moving;
  \item to \textbf{excite} is to call the movement out of somebody.
\end{itemize}

Spanish took the appearing. \textbf{Una cita} is a time somebody has been called to — with a doctor, with a lawyer, or with a person you would like to see again. The second meaning, the quotation, is the English \emph{cite} in noun form, so both halves of the Latin verb are alive in the same Spanish word.

What makes it useful is that it is the only ordinary word for a fixed appointment. \emph{La hora} gives you the number. \emph{La cita} gives you the promise.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A time that two people have agreed to, rather than one the clock happens to show.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cita}
  \item \emph{tengo una cita}
  \item \emph{una cita a las cinco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{citāre} mean in Latin? (To summon.) And what is the other thing \emph{una cita} can be? (A quotation.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la etapa]{la etapa — a storehouse that turned into a distance}

\label{lesson:ES-C356-etapa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{from}, then \emph{the appointment}. (\emph{Desde}; \emph{la cita}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el viaje — what it is a piece of.
  \item la jornada — one day of one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{e-TA-pa}, three beats with the weight on the second. Every vowel is short and clean. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la etapa} — \textquotedblleft{}a stage,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a leg\textquotedblright{} of a journey or of anything else.

The word did not start as a distance. It started as a building.

Middle Dutch \textbf{stapel} was a heap — a market pile, a stack of goods for sale. French borrowed it as \emph{estaple} for a depot: the storehouse where a marching army halted and drew its bread. Because the army stopped there, the word came to mean the \emph{march between two of them}, and once it meant that it could mean any stretch of anything: a stage of a race, a stage of a plan, a stage of a life.

English borrowed the same Dutch pile and kept it a pile. A \textbf{staple} is a main commodity, and a \emph{staple town} held the legal right to be the place where a commodity was heaped and sold.

And French did the usual thing to the \emph{s} in \emph{estaple}. It dropped it and put a mark over the vowel: \textbf{étape}. The accent is the same headstone as the little hat in \emph{hôtel} — Spanish borrowed the word after the \emph{s} had already gone.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to cut a long thing into pieces without naming a clock.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la etapa}
  \item \emph{la primera etapa}
  \item \emph{una etapa del viaje}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was an \emph{étape} before it was a distance? (A storehouse, a heap.) And which English word is the same Dutch pile? (Staple.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ocasión]{la ocasión — chance, imagined as falling}

\label{lesson:ES-C356-ocasion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the appointment}, then \emph{the stage}. (\emph{La cita}; \emph{la etapa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la suerte — its neighbour, and a different picture.
  \item la vez — the plainer word for one time.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-ka-SION}, three beats with the weight on the last, which is why it carries a written accent. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is hard. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ocasión} — \textquotedblleft{}the occasion,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the chance.\textquotedblright{}

Latin thought about luck as a falling. \textbf{Cadere} is to fall, and an \textbf{occāsiō} is a falling-down: \emph{ob-}, down, plus \emph{cadere}. What happens to you is what drops in front of you.

Once the falling is pointed out to you, it turns up everywhere:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an \textbf{accident} is what falls toward you — \emph{ad} + \emph{cadere};
  \item a \textbf{case} is how a thing fell out;
  \item \textbf{chance} is Vulgar Latin \textbf{cadentia}, the falling, worn down through French;
  \item a \textbf{cascade} falls down a hillside;
  \item a \textbf{cadence} is where a line of music falls at the end;
  \item and something \textbf{decays} by falling away.
\end{itemize}

Even the compass is in it: the \textbf{occident} is the west, because that is where the sun falls. Spanish keeps that one whole in \emph{el occidente}, sitting beside \emph{el oeste}, which is a Germanic word that came in through French.

\textbf{La ocasión} is a moment that fell your way. \emph{La suerte} is luck as a drawn lot, and \emph{la vez} is a plain turn — three pictures for three different things.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A chance, and a Latin verb that turns out to be underneath half the English words for luck.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ocasión}
  \item \emph{en esta ocasión}
  \item \emph{una buena ocasión}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{cadere} mean? (To fall.) And why is the west the \emph{occident}? (It is where the sun falls.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[de repente]{de repente — what is sudden is what crept}

\label{lesson:ES-C356-repente}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the stage}, then \emph{the occasion}. (\emph{La etapa}; \emph{la ocasión}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la demora — the opposite kind of arrival.
  \item el instante — how long it takes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de re-PEN-te}, with the weight on \emph{PEN}. Both \emph{r} sounds are single taps, not rolled. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{de repente} — \textquotedblleft{}suddenly,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}all at once.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{repēns} means sudden, and it is the present participle of \textbf{repere}, to creep. Read that twice, because it is a whole idea about surprise: the thing that startles you is the thing that came \emph{creeping}. It was on its way the whole time. You did not hear it.

\textbf{Repente} is that participle in the ablative — \textquotedblleft{}creepingly\textquotedblright{} — and Spanish locked it into the phrase \emph{de repente}.

English has \emph{repere} in one common word and it is the right one: a \textbf{reptile} is a creeper, an animal named for how it moves rather than what it is.

So Spanish has three speeds now:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la demora}, the thing that is late;
  \item \emph{el instante}, the smallest piece of time there is;
  \item and \emph{de repente}, the thing that arrives without warning after creeping up on you.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to place a thing in time: \emph{desde}, \emph{la cita}, \emph{la etapa}, \emph{la ocasión}, \emph{de repente}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de repente}
  \item \emph{desde ayer}
  \item \emph{una cita, una etapa, una ocasión}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{repere} mean? (To creep.) And which animal is named for it? (The reptile.)
\end{tcolorbox}
